title: Chapter 58: A Lord's Last Evening, Part 3 of 5: The Stone
html:
"No," said Silas.
He said it before Corin could open his mouth. He said it the way a doctor says it, flat and final, the way you shut a door. And he leaned forward over the open case, between Corin and the stone, as if he could block it with his long thin body.
"No. I told you. A hand's width. Not a candle. Not a spark."
"It isn't burning," said Corin.
"It's taking in." Silas did not move. "I know what a memory stone is. I've seen two. In the war. A tier-four stone. A whole evening of a man's life, pressed so hard it went solid. You can't pour it out like a jar. You can't hold it to the light and look. The only way to see what's in a thing like that is for a harvester to take it into himself. All of it. And walk through it, inside, from the beginning to the end." He looked at Corin's hands. "And every harvester who ever lived will tell you the same thing. What you take in leaves its mark. Same as what you burn. Ash in, gray out."
"Not as much."
"Not as much," Silas agreed. "Not as fast. But some. And you haven't got some. You've got a hand's width." His tired voice did not rise. "You took in eighty-one years of the Lady last night, on top of everything else. I can see it in your face. You've been looking at the fire all morning like a man looking at somebody else's house. You've no room left, Vane. None. Not for another man's evening. Not for an hour of it."
Corin did not answer.
He was looking at the stone. At the small gold light, deep inside it, walking round and round.
No room left.
That was not true. He knew it was not true. There was room. There was a great deal of room. There was a whole empty house, with the furniture carried out, and the Lady had moved into one corner of it, and the rest was bare. He had made room. On his knees. On the floor of the dome.
But it was not the room that worried Silas. It was the hand's width.
"There's another way," said Corin.
Silas looked at him.
"Maybe," said Corin. "There might be."
He turned, slowly, on the stone floor. Against the pillar. And reached behind him, to where his coat lay folded, Fenton's heavy coat, that Silas had taken off him in the night. And felt in the inside pocket, with the sides of his white-wrapped hands. Past the Ledger. Past the stub of pencil. To the other thing that lived there. That had lived there since Sunday.
A small thick book. Wrapped in oilcloth. Tied with string.
He held it in his lap.
The Ledger said what it was. He had read it last night by the fire, on a page from Sunday. LINUS HALE GAVE ME HIS BOOK. 62 YEARS. SINCE HE WAS 19. THE OLD SLOW WAYS. SECRET THINGS IN THE BACK, IN THE OLD LETTERS. NOT TO BE OPENED UNTIL AFTER MONDAY. I PROMISED.
It was after Monday.
He untied the string. It took a long time. His fingers would not do it. In the end the girl in the gray gown reached across and did it for him, without a word, with her cut thumb, and pulled the oilcloth back, and put the book in his hands, and sat back on her heels.
It was old. Older than anything he had ever held. The leather of the cover had gone soft and dark and smooth as skin, and the pages were yellow, and thick, and soft at the edges from sixty-two years of turning. And they were full. Every page, from the first to the last, written close and small in a slanting old-fashioned hand that changed, page by page, as he turned them. Young at the front. Firm and quick and black. Then steadier. Then slower. Then, toward the back, shaky, and pale, as if the ink had been watered, or the hand had.
He turned to the back.
And the writing changed.
Not the hand. The letters. The last twenty pages were not written in letters he knew. They were written in something older. Curling, looping shapes, joined together, with marks above and below them like small birds sitting on a wire. He looked at them and they meant nothing. Like a fence. Like ivy on a wall.
The old letters, he thought.
Turn it to the light, boy.
Malakor.
Corin held the book up to the red light of the brazier.
Further. There. Hold it there. A pause. And then, in a voice Corin had never heard from him before, low, almost wondering: Saints. He kept it. All of it. The old hand. Corvell's hand. I haven't seen this written since—
He stopped.
Can you read it?
I wrote half of it, said Malakor.
Corin sat very still.
Not this book, said Malakor. The book he copied it from. Corvell's. In the old Harvesting rooms. Under the Ministry. Before it was the Ministry. I was the one who wrote the slow ways down, boy. Me. Seventy years ago and more. So that they wouldn't be lost. And Corvell kept the book, and gave it to Linus when he was nineteen, and Linus copied it out in the back of his own, in the old letters, so nobody would read it who shouldn't. A dry sound that might have been a laugh. And here it is. In a crypt. In your lap.
What does it say?
Turn the pages. Slowly. I'll tell you when.
Corin turned the pages.
One. Two. Five. Eight. The curling looping shapes went past, meaning nothing. The girl watched him. So did Silas. So did Gideon, against his father's side, with his head on one side, the way he looked at chalk marks.
Stop.
Corin stopped.
It was a page near the very end. The shapes on it looked like all the others. But at the top, in the margin, there was a small drawing. Very small. In faded ink. A round stone, like an egg. And beside it, two hands. One holding the other.
There, said Malakor. Read it to them. Say it after me.
And Corin read it to them. Aloud. In Fenton's voice, which was not quite his own. Word by word, after the dry old voice behind his left ear.
"To walk a stone, and not keep it.
"A stone is a whole thing, and will not be poured. It must be walked. The harvester walks it as he walks a dream, from the beginning to the end, and at the end he wakes, and it is in him. This is the common way, and it is a heavy way, and it leaves its mark.
"But there is a lighter way, which is older. It is this.
"Let the harvester lie down, and put the stone on his brow, and shut his eyes. And let one of the blood of the one in the stone hold his hand. For the stone knows its own blood, and the blood is a rope, and the stone will not take the harvester all the way in while the rope is held.
"So the harvester will not walk the stone. He will walk beside it. He will see all of it, and feel all of it, as a man sees and feels a thing through a window. But it will not come into him, and it will not stay.
"And when it is time, let the one who holds the rope call him back. By his name. In a voice he knows. For the blood calls the stone, but only the name calls the walker. And if there is no voice he knows, he will not hear, and he will not come back, and the stone will keep him."
Corin stopped.
He read the last line again. To himself. In his own head. And then he lowered the book, slowly, into his lap.
The crypt was very quiet.
In a voice he knows.
Boy, said Malakor. Very gently. Now you know why I told you not to spend it.
Corin did not say anything.
He looked across the open case, across the stone with its small gold light walking round and round, at the girl in the gray gown.
She was looking at him.
She had heard it. Every word. One of the blood of the one in the stone. That was her. In a voice he knows. That was—
He did not know her face. He did not know her name, except from the book. He did not know the sound of her step, or what she looked like when she laughed, or what she had been to him.
But he knew her voice.
One thing. In the last corner of the empty room. A voice, saying his name. A little quick. A little cross. As if he were late for something.
He had kept it.
He had not known why. On the roof, he had said I don't know why I kept that. Malakor had said You don't have to spend that one, and he had not, and he had not known why that mattered.
It was for this.
The girl's face did not change. But she put her hand flat on the stone floor beside the case. As if to hold herself up.
"He means me," she said.
"Yes," said Corin.
"The blood is me. And the voice is me."
"Yes."
She was quiet for a moment.
"You kept my voice," she said. "So that I could call you back."
"I didn't know," said Corin. "When I kept it. I didn't know what it was for." He looked down at Linus's book in his lap, at the small faded drawing in the margin of a stone and two hands, one holding the other. "Malakor knew. I think. I didn't."
She looked at him for a long time.
Then she looked away, at the fire.
"Rule one," she said, to the fire. "No lies between us. Not even the kind ones." She swallowed. "Is it dangerous? This way. The lighter way."
Tell her, said Malakor.
"If you let go," said Corin, "or if you don't call, or if I don't hear, the stone keeps me. That's what it says."
"And if I hold on, and I call, and you hear?"
"Then I come back. And I've seen it. And it doesn't stay. And the gray doesn't come." He looked at Silas. "Not much."
Silas took off his spectacles. And rubbed his eyes with the back of his wrist. And put them back on, crooked.
"It's the old slow way," he said. "Isn't it. From that book. The kind that Linus Hale kept." His tired voice was very quiet. "He came here on Sunday, you know. Up the lane with his stick. To give you that. He could hardly get up the steps. I gave him tea." He looked down. "I'd heard what he did. To Lord Thorne. To others. I didn't want to give him tea. I gave him tea."
He was quiet.
"All right," he said. "The slow way. But if your hands start to go, if the gray moves, even a finger's width, I'll pull the stone off your head myself. Do you understand? I don't care what's in it."
"Yes."
Silas nodded, and moved back out of the way.
Corin lay down.
On the stone floor of the crypt. On his back. By the fire. With Fenton's coat folded under his head for a pillow, and his bad leg out straight, and his strangers' hands on his chest. He looked up at the round stone arches, red in the firelight, like the inside of a loaf.
The girl in the gray gown took the stone out of the case.
She held it for a moment in both hands. Looking at it. At the small gold light, walking round and round. Corin saw her lips move. Not counting. Something else. He could not hear.
Then she knelt beside him, on his right side. And put the stone on his forehead. Very gently. In the middle, just above his eyes.
It was warm.
He had thought it would be cold. It was warm. Warm like a hand. Like somebody's palm, laid on his forehead, the way you lay your hand on a child's head to feel for fever.
And she took his right hand. In both of hers. His slate-gray hand, with the white linen on its black fingertips. She held it against her, in her lap. Tight.
He could not feel her fingers. Not on the black ends of his own. But he could feel her hands round the gray of his palm. Like through a glove. A little.
It was enough.
I'm here, said Malakor. Behind his left ear. I'll be the other rope. If she lets go, I won't.
You never said that before.
I never had a rope before.
The girl leaned over him. Close. He could see her face upside down, above him, against the red stone of the arches. Dark eyes. Sharp chin. The small worried line between her brows.
"Corin," she said.
And he knew it.
Not her. The voice. The shape of it. Quick. A little cross. The last thing in the last corner.
"That's it," he said. "That's the one."
She did not say anything. Her hands tightened round his.
Corin shut his eyes.
And the warm stone on his forehead opened like a door.
Crown Walk, Two Autumns Gone
Rain.
That was first. The sound of it. Rain on a window, steady and soft, the way rain falls in the autumn when it has made up its mind to fall all night. And a fire. The small busy crackle of a coal fire in a grate. And a clock, somewhere behind him, ticking. Slow. Deep. A tall clock, in a tall case, the kind that stands in the corner of a room and has stood there for a hundred years.
And then the room came.
It came the way a room comes when you open your eyes in the morning. All at once. Not seen. Known. He knew it the way you know your own bedroom in the dark. Every corner. Every chair. Where the floor creaked. Which drawer stuck.
It was a study. Not large. Square, and warm, and lined with books from the floor to the ceiling on three sides, old books in brown and red and green leather, with gold on their spines worn down to nothing by hands. On the fourth side, a window. Tall, with heavy curtains of dark green velvet drawn half across it, and the rain running down the black glass beyond, and in the glass, faint, the reflection of the fire. A desk by the window, big and dark and old, with papers on it in neat piles and a brass lamp with a green shade. A fire in a fireplace of plain gray stone, with a fender of brass and a basket of coal. Two chairs by the fire, deep and old, in worn brown leather. A rug, red and blue, worn thin in front of the fire where feet had rested on it for years. And the clock. In the corner, by the door. Tall and dark, with a pale face, and a moon on the face that showed the time of the month.
He was sitting in one of the chairs.
The one on the left. The one with the dip in the seat, that fitted him. With a book open on his knee, and his feet on the worn place in the rug, and a glass on the small table at his elbow with an inch of something dark and red in it that he had not drunk.
Corin knew it was not him.
He knew that the way you know, in a dream, that you are dreaming. Somewhere very far away, behind him, below him, there was a stone floor, and a fire in a brazier, and a warm stone on his forehead, and two hands holding his. He could not feel them. But he knew they were there. A rope. Going back.
And here, in the study, in the chair, he was somebody else.
He looked down at the hands holding the book.
They were not gray. That was the first thing. They were a man's hands, long and thin and pale, with the knuckles a little swollen, the way a man's knuckles swell after fifty. Clean. No ink. No gray. On the third finger of the left hand, a ring. Plain gold. Worn thin. And on the little finger of the right hand, another ring. Heavier. A signet. With a crest cut into the flat gold face. A tree, with a crown in its branches.
The Thorne crest. He knew it. Not from the Ledger. From here. From the man whose hands these were. He had worn that ring since his father died. Thirty-one years.
Aurelian.
That was the name. Not Lord Thorne. Nobody in this house called him that, except Bertram, and only in front of guests. Aurelian. That was what his mother had called him. And his wife.
His wife.
Corin felt it. The way you feel a draft from a door that has been left open in another room. A cold place. In the middle of the man. Small. Old. Nine years old. A place where somebody had been, and was not. And the man in the chair did not look at it. He had not looked at it for nine years. He walked round it, every day, the way you walk round a hole in a floor.
Isolde.
And then the man in the chair thought of something else, quickly, the way you look away from a light that hurts your eyes. And Corin went with him.
Upstairs.
The man was thinking about upstairs. About the two rooms on the second floor, at the end of the passage, with their doors shut and a line of candlelight under each one. He could not see them. But he knew they were there. The way you know where your hand is in the dark.
The left-hand door. Rowan's. A boy of sixteen, who had come home from the Collegium on Thursday for the autumn holiday, taller than he had been in the spring, with his voice broken and his shoulders gone broad and his face gone closed. Who had said Good evening, Father, at supper, and Yes, Father, and No, Father, and nothing else at all, and gone up to his room at the eighth bell and shut the door. The man in the chair thought about the boy's shut door, and something in his chest went tight and sore, like a bruise when you press it.
He thinks I don't see him. He thinks I don't care. He's sixteen and his mother's been gone nine years and his father reads books by the fire every night and never says anything that matters. The thought was very clear. Very tired. And he's right.
And the right-hand door.
Corin felt the man's whole body change when he thought of it. Not tighten. Loosen. The way your shoulders come down when you walk into a warm room out of the cold.
Lyra.
The name went through the man in the chair like warmth through a cold hand.
And with it came a picture. Not a memory. A picture the man was holding, in the front of his mind, the way you hold a letter you have read so many times you no longer need to look at the words. A girl. Eighteen. Sitting on the bottom stair of the front hall that very evening, before supper, with her shoes off and her stockinged feet on the cold marble and a book in her lap. Reading. Frowning at it. With her long dark hair coming down out of its pins at one side, the way it always did, however Mrs. Hobb pinned it. And looking up, as he came across the hall, with her finger in the book to keep her place, and saying: Father. Did you know there are fourteen stairs to the first landing? I've counted them every day since I was nine. There have always been fourteen. And he had said: Have you, my dear? And she had said: Yes. Every day. I don't know why. And looked down at her book again. And he had stood there in the hall and not been able to say anything, because he knew why, and she did not, and he had promised her mother he would never tell her.
Corin lay inside the man's memory, in the chair, by the fire, in the rain, and felt it.
He felt what the man felt. That was the thing. That was what the slow way meant. He did not only see. He felt. The way you feel the heat of a fire through a window. And what the man in the chair felt, holding that picture of a girl on a stair with her shoes off, counting, was—
Corin did not have a word for it.
He had words for most things. He had been a Senior Investigator of the Ministry of Records for ten years. He had words for fear and rage and grief and shame and greed, he had harvested all of them out of other people's Ash, he had felt them go through him and filed them in the Ledger under their names. He had words for love, even. The ordinary kinds. A man for a woman. A woman for a man. A child for a dog.
He did not have a word for this.
It was bigger than him. Bigger than the man in the chair. It filled the man the way the sea fills a harbor at high tide, all the way up, into every corner, lifting everything, so that the man in the chair was only a boat floating on it. It was quiet. It did not shout. It did not need to. It had been there for eighteen years, since the morning the girl was born, and it had never once gone out, not for a day, not for an hour, not even in the nine years since her mother went, when the man had gone out of almost everything else.
It was not proud. It was not anxious. It did not want anything from her. It only wanted her to be. To go on being. To sit on the bottom stair with her shoes off and her hair coming down and count the stairs to the first landing every day for the rest of her life, and be safe, and never know why.
That's what he feels, thought Corin. For her.
For the girl holding my hand.
He did not know her.
But her father did. And for as long as the stone lasted, Corin was her father. And he lay in the dark behind the man's eyes, in the warm study, in the rain, two years gone, and felt what it was to love the girl in the gray gown so much that you would have walked into a fire for her without stopping to look for the door.
He had walked into a fire for her. Last night. He had read it in the Ledger. He had walked into the Bourse on one leg and held up the sky.
He had not known, until now, what it must have felt like from inside.
The tall clock in the corner struck.
Eight. Deep and slow. Each stroke falling into the warm room like a stone into a well.
And the man in the chair closed his book.
He did it slowly, and laid it on the small table beside the untouched glass. And sat with his long pale hands on the arms of the chair, looking at the fire. And Corin felt the warmth go out of him. All at once. The way warmth goes out of a room when somebody opens the door onto the night.
Because the man was not reading.
He had not been reading all evening. Corin understood that now. The book had been open on his knee since supper, and he had not turned a page. He had been sitting by the fire with an open book and an untouched glass and the rain on the window, thinking about his children, upstairs, behind their shut doors, the way a man thinks about his children when he does not know if he will see them again.
He was waiting.
For somebody to come.
And he was afraid.
Corin felt the fear come up in the man like cold water coming up through the floor of a cellar. Slow. Steady. From a long way down. Not a sudden fear. An old one. A fear the man had been carrying for a long time, years, and had got used to, the way you get used to a stone in your shoe. And tonight, at last, he was going to take the stone out.
There was a knock at the door of the study.
Soft. Two knocks.
"Come," said the man in the chair. His voice was deep and quiet and quite steady. Corin felt it in his own throat.
The door opened.
An old man in black stood in it. Small and round and very neat, with white side-whiskers and a bald pink head and a face like a kind owl. A butler. Bertram. Thirty years in this house. Corin knew that too, the way the man in the chair knew it.
"My lord," said Bertram. "There is a person at the garden door."
The man in the chair did not move.
"A person," he said.
"Yes, my lord." Bertram's kind owl face was quite blank. "In a traveling cloak. Very wet. Who gives no name. Who asks me to say to your lordship only this." He paused, as a good butler pauses before a message he has been asked to give word for word. "The dark is the day with its eyes shut."
And the man in the chair shut his eyes.
Corin felt it. Felt the words go into him like a key into a lock. And turn. And something open, deep in the man, that had been shut for a very long time.
"Bring them in, Bertram," said Lord Aurelian Thorne. "By the garden way. Not the hall. And then go to bed. And if anybody asks you, in the morning, or any morning, who came to this house tonight, you will say that nobody came."
Bertram bowed.
"Nobody came, my lord," he said.
And went out, and shut the door.
